*'''10''' teams appeared in every World Cup:
*{{ru|SAM}}/Western Samoa also qualified for every World Cup but was not invited to the [[1987 Rugby World Cup]]. 
*{{ru|RSA}} was banned from competing in [[1987 Rugby World Cup|1987]] and [[1991 Rugby World Cup|1991]] due to the [[Sporting boycott of South Africa during the apartheid era|sporting boycott of South Africa]], but appeared in every World Cup since the ban was lifted.

'''Oldest player to appear in a World Cup match'''
*[[Diego Ormaechea]], {{ru|URU}}, aged {{age in years and days|1959|9|19|1999|10|15}} (v {{ru|RSA}}, [[1999 Rugby World Cup#Pool A|15 October 1999]])<ref name="Griffiths 2011-09-12">{{cite web|url=http://www.espnscrum.com/2011-rugby-world-cup/rugby/story/148929.html |title=Victors in the Five/Six Nations, Tri-Nations and the World Cup, the youngest and oldest players, referees and close encounters |first=John |last=Griffiths |work=Ask John |publisher=ESPN Scrum |date=12 September 2011 |access-date=13 September 2011}}</ref><ref>For the specific match where Ormaeches established the current record, see the [http://www.espnscrum.com/statsguru/rugby/player/11594.html?class=1;orderby=date;orderbyad=reverse;template=results;type=player;view=match list of his Test matches] at ESPN Scrum.</ref>

'''Oldest player to appear in a World Cup final'''
*[[Duane Vermeulen]], {{ru|RSA}}, aged {{age in years and days|1986|7|3|2023|10|28}} (v {{ru|NZL}}, [[2023 Rugby World Cup final|28 October 2023]])

'''Oldest player to win a World Cup final'''
*[[Schalk Brits]], {{ru|RSA}}, aged {{age in years and days|1981|5|16|2019|11|02}} (v {{ru|ENG}}, [[2019 Rugby World Cup final|2 November 2019]])

'''Youngest player to appear in a World Cup match'''
*[[Vasil Lobzhanidze]], {{ru|GEO}}, aged {{age in years and days|1996|10|14|2015|9|19}} (v {{ru|TGA}}, [[2015 Rugby World Cup Pool C#Tonga vs Georgia|19 September 2015]])<ref>{{cite web|url=http://en.espn.co.uk/scrum/rugby/story/275225.html |title=Georgia spring first surprise by taking down Tonga |agency=[[Press Association|PA Sport]] |publisher=[[ESPN (UK)]] |date=19 September 2015 |access-date=19 September 2015}}</ref>

'''Youngest player to appear in a World Cup final'''
*[[Jonah Lomu]], {{ru|NZL}}, aged {{age in years and days|1975|5|12|1995|6|24}} (v {{ru|RSA}}, [[1995 Rugby World Cup final|24 June 1995]])<ref name="Griffiths 2011-09-12"/>

'''Youngest player to win a World Cup final'''
*[[François Steyn]], {{ru|RSA}}, aged {{age in years and days|1987|5|14|2007|10|20}} (v {{ru|ENG}}, [[2007 Rugby World Cup final|20 October 2007]])<ref name="Griffiths 2011-09-12"/>

*89,267 – {{ru|Ireland}} v {{ru|Romania}}, 27 September [[2015 Rugby World Cup Pool D#Ireland vs Romania|2015]] at [[Wembley Stadium]], London, England<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stats.espnscrum.com/scrum/rugby/records/team/highest_attendance.html?id=17;type=trophy |title=Rugby World Cup - Highest attendance |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=2 November 2019 |access-date=2 November 2019}}</ref>

* 82,957 – {{ru|Australia}} v {{ru|England}}, 22 November [[2003 Rugby World Cup final|2003]] at [[Stadium Australia]], Sydney, Australia<ref>[https://www.austadiums.com/sport/event/1071 2003 Rugby World Cup Final]</ref>

=== Lowest attendance ===
*2,000 – {{ru|Argentina}} v {{ru|Italy}}, 28 May [[1987 Rugby World Cup Pool 3|1987]] at [[Lancaster Park]], Christchurch, New Zealand

=== Hosting ===
[[File:Eden_Park_cropped.jpg|thumbnail|Eden Park was the first stadium to host the World Cup Final twice.]]

*[[Eden Park]] in [[Auckland]] Park was the first stadium to host the [[Rugby World Cup Final]] twice, with the 1987 and 2011 finals having been held there. [[Twickenham Stadium]] has also hosted the final twice in 1991 and 2015, as has the [[Stade de France]] in 2007 and 2023.
*The record for the city that has been a part of the most Rugby World Cups is currently four, and is held by [[Cardiff]], which hosted matches in [[1991 Rugby World Cup|1991]], [[1999 Rugby World Cup|1999]], [[2007 Rugby World Cup|2007]] and [[2015 Rugby World Cup|2015]]. If the definition of "city" includes its metropolitan area, [[Paris]] has also hosted matches in four tournaments. Paris hosted matches in 1991; its adjacent suburb of [[Saint-Denis, Seine-Saint-Denis|Saint-Denis]] hosted matches in 1999 and 2023; and both cities hosted matches in 2007. [[Edinburgh]] and [[Toulouse]] have hosted matches in three tournaments.

=== Head-to-head ===
The highest number of head-to-head matches between two nations currently stands at eight, encompassing four teams ([[Australia national rugby union team|Australia]], [[France national rugby union team|France]], [[New Zealand national rugby union team|New Zealand]], and [[Wales national rugby union team|Wales]]) in two [[Rugby World Cup]] [[Rivalry#Sports|rivalries]]. The following table lists the head-to-head statistics of the Rugby World Cup, ranging from the inaugural tournament in [[1987 Rugby World Cup|1987]] to the latest tournament in [[2023 Rugby World Cup|2023]]. ==== Tier 1 nations head-to-head ====
The table below shows the current dominance in the head-to-head meetings of Tier 1 nations at the [[Rugby World Cup]] from the first tournament in [[1987 Rugby World Cup|1987]] to the latest tournament in [[2023 Rugby World Cup|2023]] (as of 20 October). Currently, [[New Zealand national rugby union team|New Zealand]] has the best record amongst the other Tier 1 nations, achieving more wins and culminating in a superior head-to-head record over seven other Tier 1 nations, and equal with two others ([[Australia national rugby union team|Australia]] and [[South Africa national rugby union team|South Africa]]). [[Italy national rugby union team|Italy]] are at the bottom of the table, and have an inferior head-to-head record with eight other Tier 1 nations, and parity with one other nation ([[Argentina national rugby union team|Argentina]]). However, as of the 2023 tournament Japan are the bottom team. There are two Tier 1 head-to-head meetings that have never been played at a Rugby World Cup: [[England national rugby union team|England]]–[[Ireland national rugby union team|Ireland]], and [[Scotland national rugby union team|Scotland]]–[[Wales national rugby union team|Wales]].

=== Trivia ===
*England became the first sole host nation to be eliminated in the pool stage of a [[Rugby World Cup]] in 2015. Wales, as joint hosts, were eliminated in the pool stage in 1991.
*Four match-ups have occurred twice in the same World Cup:
**2007 Argentina defeated France in the opening match 17–12, and went on to beat them 34–10 in the bronze final. 
**2007 South Africa defeated England 36–0 in the pool stage, and went on to play them in the final, winning 15–6. 
**2011 New Zealand defeated France 37–17 in the pool stage, and went on to play them in the final, winning 8–7.
**2023 England defeated Argentina 27–10 in the pool stage, and went on to beat them 26–23 in the bronze final.
*There are two tier 1 head-to-head meetings that have never been played at a [[Rugby World Cup]]: [[England national rugby union team|England]] versus [[Ireland national rugby union team|Ireland]], and [[Scotland national rugby union team|Scotland]] versus [[Wales national rugby union team|Wales]].
*Four nations have reached a [[Rugby World Cup Final]] having previously lost a game in that tournament: England in 1991 and 2007, South Africa in 2019 and 2023, New Zealand in 2023 and France in 2011, the latter being the only team to reach the final having lost two games. The 2023 final is the only one with both teams having previously lost a game in the tournament.
*New Zealand have been involved in four World Cup opening matches, the most by any other team. The All Blacks defeated Italy in 1987, England in 1991, and Tonga in 2011, but lost to France in 2023. Argentina have participated in three World Cup opening matches. The Pumas participated in the first three World Cup openers of the professional era – losing to Wales and Australia in 1999 and 2003 respectively, and defeating France in 2007.
*France and New Zealand are the only nations to have made it to at least the quarter-finals of every Rugby World Cup. Furthermore, South Africa have also done so since they started participating in 1995.
*France is the only non English-speaking country to have made it to a Rugby World Cup final – in 1987, 1999 and 2011. It is also the only country to reach a final without ever winning it.
*The only Tier 2 country to have participated in every Rugby World Cup is Japan, with Canada only failing to qualify for the first time in 2023, making it to one quarter-final in 1991 and Japan reaching the quarter finals in 2019. 
*Japan is the only team to have won three matches in a tournament where they did not progress beyond the pool stage, losing out to South Africa and Scotland in their pool by points difference in 2015.
*Among the Tier 1 nations, Italy is the only one not to have made it to at least the quarter-finals in any Rugby World Cup. Conversely, four Tier 2 countries have made it to the quarter-finals – Fiji in 1987, 2007 and 2023, Samoa (then called Western Samoa) in 1991 and 1995, Canada in 1991 and Japan in 2019. 
**Arguably, Argentina in 1999 could also be regarded as having been a Tier 2 nation at the time, since they were not yet in the southern-hemisphere Rugby Championship: although official "Tiers" were not recognised at the time, this match can be regarded as the start of their actual period of achievement which led to them later earning recognition at the top table. Similarly, Japan's achievements in 2019, added to their defeat of South Africa in 2015, were eventually recognised by formally admitting them to the definition of a Tier 1 nation in May 2023.
*The [[2015 Rugby World Cup Final|2015 final]] between Australia and New Zealand is the highest scoring Rugby World Cup final, with New Zealand winning that match 34–17.
*After the [[2015 Rugby World Cup Final|2015 final]], New Zealand became the first team to win the Rugby World Cup three times, and the first team to have successfully defended its title. South Africa became the second team to defend its title in [[2023 Rugby World Cup Final|2023]] and the first to win the Rugby World Cup on four occasions, as well as the first to win successive titles away from home.
*Wales have had the most upsets in the Rugby World Cup, having lost to Samoa both in 1991 and 1999, then losing to Fiji in 2007. Other major upsets include Ireland and Scotland losing to Japan in 2019, France losing to Tonga in 2011, South Africa losing to Japan in 2015 and Australia losing to Fiji in 2023. Argentina's defeat of Ireland in 1999 was also regarded as an upset at the time.
*South Africa became the first nation to win a World Cup after losing a match in the pool stage in 2019 and did so again in 2023.
*Scotland were the last Tier 1 team to experience defeat in the pool stages of a Rugby World Cup. They were defeated by [[Ireland national rugby union team|Ireland]] in [[2023 Rugby World Cup|2023]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/67043564 |title=Rugby World Cup: Ireland 36-14 Scotland - Imperious Irish crush Scots to reach quarter-finals |publisher=[[BBC]] |date=8 September 2023 |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref>
